contactPage.faqTitle: Questions we are usually asked first

faq.question: What size of engagement do you take on?
faq.answer: From a two-week discovery sprint to a multi-month build. What matters more than size is whether the outcome is definable — if nobody can say what success looks like, that is the first piece of work.

faq.question: Do you work fixed-price or time-and-materials?
faq.answer: Both. Fixed price suits work whose scope is genuinely settled, which is rarer than people expect. Otherwise an agreed capacity with reviewed scope gives you the same budget control without pricing in the risk of guessing wrong.

faq.question: Can you work with our existing team?
faq.answer: Yes. A good deal of our work is embedded alongside an in-house team, to their process and standards. We are equally comfortable owning a delivery end to end.

faq.question: Do you sign NDAs and work under our security requirements?
faq.answer: Routinely. Most of our references are in banking, central banking and the public sector, so contractual and security review is a normal part of starting work rather than an obstacle to it.

faq.question: Where are you based, and does it matter?
faq.answer: We work remotely with clients across Europe and are used to regulated environments where data residency and access control are contractual. If your project requires on-site presence, say so and we will tell you honestly whether we can meet it.

howWeWorkPage.seoDescription: Framing, sprints, production and run — how Next Level Code delivers software, with the quality and security commitments that come with it.
howWeWorkPage.title: A method built around being wrong early
howWeWorkPage.lead: Every engagement is an argument about what should exist. The point of the process is to make that argument cheap to lose at the start, when changing direction costs a conversation, rather than expensive to lose at the end.

phases.title: Four stages, each ending in something you can judge

items.title: Framing
items.body: We establish what is true before agreeing what to build: the systems in scope, the constraints that are not negotiable, the people who will operate the result, and the outcome that would count as success. It ends in a plan specific enough to cost.
items.output: A costed plan, a named architecture, and the risks ranked

items.title: Sprints
items.body: Short cycles against working software. You see the real thing at every step — not a mock-up — early enough that changing your mind is still cheap. Scope is reviewed at each boundary rather than defended.
items.output: Working software at the end of every cycle

items.title: Production
items.body: Deployment, security review, observability and operational handover are part of the build, not a phase that follows it. A system that works only on the machine that built it is not finished.
items.output: Running under real load, with monitoring you can read

items.title: Run
items.body: Support, evolution and the transfer of ownership to your team: documentation, walkthroughs and the code review habits that let them take it on. A permanent dependency on us is not a successful outcome.
items.output: Your team able to change the system without us

items.title: Tests where they earn their keep
items.body: Coverage of the logic that carries risk, not a percentage target. A suite nobody trusts is worse than no suite, because it is still slow.

items.title: Review before merge, always
items.body: Every change is read by someone other than its author. It is the cheapest defect-finding mechanism in software and the first one teams abandon under pressure.

items.title: Decisions written down
items.body: Architecture choices are recorded with the alternatives and the reasoning, so a future maintainer inherits the argument rather than just the outcome.

items.title: No silent scope
items.body: If something is going to take longer or cost more, you hear it when we find out, not at the end. Bad news does not improve with age.

security.title: Practices that apply to every engagement
items: Least privilege by default: access is granted for a task and a period, not held indefinitely.
Secrets never live in source control; credentials are rotated on handover as a matter of course.
Dependencies are pinned and monitored, and upgrades are treated as routine work rather than emergencies.
Personal data handling is decided in the design phase, because retrofitting it onto a live system is expensive and sometimes impossible.
Anything we build to run in production is reviewed against the security expectations of your sector, not ours.

communication.title: How the engagement actually feels
communication.body: You have direct access to the people writing the code — no account layer between a question and the person who can answer it. A written update every week covering what moved, what did not, and what is next. A live review at every sprint boundary. And an honest answer when you ask whether something is worth doing, including when it is not.

items.title: Weekly

items.title: Every sprint
items.body: A live review against working software, not a status deck.

items.title: Always
items.body: Direct access to the engineers, in your channel of choice.

aboutPage.seoDescription: Next Level Code is a founder-led software practice, delivering custom software, applied AI and commercial APIs for banks, public institutions and enterprises.
aboutPage.title: A small practice built for consequential systems
aboutPage.lead: Next Level Code exists because the software that matters most to an organisation is rarely the software that is easiest to buy. It has to fit an estate that already exists, satisfy people who did not ask for it, and keep working after everyone involved has moved on.

model.title: Founder-led, delivered by a collective
model.body: Founded in {foundedYear}, Next Level Code is a founder-led practice. Our projects are delivered by a hand-picked collective of software architects, senior engineers and AI specialists, led by the founder — assembled for the shape of each engagement rather than staffed from a bench.
model.rationale: That structure is deliberate. It means the people on your project were chosen for it, that the person accountable for the outcome is also close enough to the work to see it going wrong, and that we can say no to engagements we are not right for. The trade is that we take on fewer projects at once — which is the point.

items.title: The estate as it is, not as it should be
items.body: Every interesting system has history. Treating that history as an obstacle to be cleared is how modernisation projects fail; treating it as the design constraint is how they land.

items.title: Boring where it counts
items.body: We use well-understood technology for the parts that must not fail, and spend the novelty budget where it creates advantage. Interesting infrastructure is a liability someone inherits.

items.title: Written for the next reader
items.body: Code is read far more often than it is written, usually by someone with less context and less time. That reader is who we optimise for.

items.title: An honest no
items.body: We will tell you when a project should be smaller, delayed, bought instead of built, or not done. It costs us revenue and it is the reason clients come back.
